title: Sharks Can Feel Your Heartbeat. Could You Survive?
credits: Wikimedia Commons: Godot13 (CC BY-SA 4.0); Bernard Dupont (CC BY-SA 2.0); Hermanus Backpackers (CC BY 2.0); Pterantula (CC BY 2.5); Brocken Inaglory (CC BY-SA 3.0); Sharkcrew (CC BY-SA 4.0); kallerna (CC BY-SA 4.0); Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (public domain); Mdomingoa (CC BY-SA 4.0); Assianir (CC BY-SA 4.0); Luca Oddone (CC BY-SA 3.0); Australian Museum (CC BY 4.0). Video footage: Pixabay (free license).

scenes.text: You have just fallen off the boat. Before you see anything, a great white shark below has already found you. How? Stay with me, because the answer starts with your own heartbeat.
label: GREAT WHITE SHARK
Carcharodon carcharias

scenes.text: Today you are in the water off South Africa, where great whites patrol. We follow the shark second by second, and at the end one number flips who the real predator is.
label: OFF SOUTH AFRICA
Great white territory

scenes.text: First, smell. A great white's nostrils are only for smelling. Water flows through them, and even a trace of blood or fish oil can make the shark turn its head. The famous idea of one drop of blood from miles away, though, is a myth.
scenes.fact: Shark nostrils are for smelling only,\Nnever for breathing.
label: SENSE 1: SMELL
Traces of blood and oil

scenes.text: Next, pressure. Along each flank runs the lateral line, a row of sensors that feel vibrations in the water. Your kicking legs send out the same kind of ripples as a struggling fish, and a shark can feel them from some distance away.
label: SENSE 2: LATERAL LINE
Feels pressure waves

scenes.question: What are these dots?
scenes.heading: A SHARK'S SNOUT
scenes.text: Then comes the sense that gives you away. Look at the snout. Those dots are pores leading to the ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled canals that detect electric fields. Your heartbeat and muscles leak a faint field, and sharks can sense just a few billionths of a volt per centimeter.

scenes.question: Heartbeat range?
scenes.text: Quick question. How close must a shark be?
This sense works only at close range, roughly within a meter. So by the time the shark can feel your heart, it is already in the final moments of its approach, and you still have not seen a thing.

Now it rises. Great whites usually hunt from below. A seal at the surface is a dark shape against bright light, while the shark's grey back vanishes into the dark water. From beneath, you are easy to see, and it is almost invisible.
label: COUNTERSHADING
Dark back, pale belly

scenes.text: Here is the mistake. From below, a surfer paddling on a board, arms and legs dangling, can look a lot like a seal. The leading hypothesis is that most bites on surfers are mistaken identity, not hunting humans.
scenes.fact: Seen from below, a surfer on a board\Ncan resemble a seal: leading theory.

scenes.text: If the target is at the surface, the attack can be explosive. Off South Africa, great whites have been filmed launching their whole body out of the water while hitting seals. A shark that heavy reaches top speed in seconds, and the water gives you no warning.

Then, the bite. In a 2008 study, researchers digitally modeled great white jaws and estimated a bite force near eighteen thousand newtons in a very large shark, nearly two tonnes of force pressing down.

scenes.label: ABOUT 300 SERRATED TEETH
scenes.text: Around three hundred serrated teeth sit in several rows, and when one breaks, a replacement moves forward from behind. Now the good news. Many bites are a single test bite, after which the shark lets go. One idea is that a bony human is not the fat-rich seal it wants.
scenes.fact: Great whites replace lost teeth\Nfrom the rows behind them.

scenes.text: Here is the part people get wrong. The teeth are not the main danger, blood loss is. A deep bite on a limb can cut major blood vessels, and severe bleeding becomes life-threatening within minutes. Survivors are the people who get to help fast.
label: THE REAL DANGER
Blood loss, not teeth
scenes.fact: Quick pressure on a bleeding wound\Nis the first step in first aid.

scenes.text: So how dangerous is it, really? The International Shark Attack File records only a few dozen to about seventy unprovoked bites worldwide in a typical year, from all shark species, and usually fewer than ten deaths. Millions of people swim, dive and surf every year.

So what do you do if it circles? Do not thrash, and do not turn your back. Stay calm, keep the shark in sight, because some research suggests sharks are less likely to approach when they see they are watched, and move steadily toward the boat. If it makes contact, strike the eyes, nose or gills, then get out.
label: BLACKTIP REEF SHARK
Different species, same instincts
scenes.fact: Swim in groups, avoid splashing,\Nand leave the water if a shark is seen.

scenes.text: Now, the number I promised. A 2013 study in Marine Policy estimated that humans kill roughly one hundred million sharks a year, with a range of sixty-three to two hundred seventy-three million, mostly in fisheries.
Sharks kill about ten people or fewer in a year. In this story, you were never the prey. Statistically, you are the predator.

Humans are the predator. So which scares you more: the shark below, or the number above? Tell me in the comments. If this changed how you see the ocean, subscribe to Oddly Logical Science, and watch another video from the channel right now.
A shark knows you're there before you see it, and it doesn't use its eyes.
label: SHARKS FEEL YOUR HEARTBEAT
Yes, really

scenes.text: Around a shark's snout are tiny pores called ampullae of Lorenzini. They detect the weak electric fields that every living body gives off.
label: CATSHARK SNOUT PORES
Ampullae of Lorenzini

scenes.text: Their electric sense can pick up a few billionths of a volt per centimeter. Even these aquarium sharks are reading the faint electric fields around them.
So your heartbeat is not a secret. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.
From below, this surfer looks like dinner.
label: SHARKS THINK SURFERS ARE SEALS
Or do they?

scenes.text: From above it's a surfer. From below, it's a seal.
label: VIEW FROM BELOW
Surfers on boards

scenes.text: A paddling surfer, arms and legs dangling, can look a lot like a seal. Scientists think many bites on surfers are mistaken identity, often a single test bite.
So the shark was not hunting you. It was hunting a seal. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

shorts.title: A Shark Never Runs Out of Teeth

scenes.text: This mouth will never run out of teeth.
label: SAND TIGER SHARK
Teeth in rows

scenes.text: Sharks do not have one set of teeth. Behind the front row, new teeth wait in rows, ready to move forward like a conveyor belt.
Over a lifetime, one shark can go through thousands of teeth, which is why shark teeth are among the most common fossils. The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

youtube.title: Sharks Can Feel Your Heartbeat. Could You Survive?
youtube.description:
You fall off a boat with a great white shark below. How does it find you, how does it attack, how hard does it bite, what actually kills, and what do the real numbers say? We follow the encounter second by second, from smell and the electric sense that can feel a heartbeat to the real odds, and a twist about who the real predator is.

In this video:
- How do great white sharks find you?
- Why do sharks mistake surfers for seals?
- How strong is a great white bite?
- What actually kills in a shark bite?
- How rare are shark attacks?
- What should you do if a shark circles you?

FAQ
Can sharks sense a heartbeat? They detect weak electric fields from muscles and heart at close range, roughly a meter.
How strong is a great white bite? A 2008 model estimated about 18,000 newtons in a very large shark.
How many sharks do humans kill? A 2013 study estimated about 100 million a year (63 to 273 million).

Sources:
- NOAA Fisheries, great white shark species profile
- Florida Museum, International Shark Attack File (annual worldwide summaries)
- Wroe et al. 2008, 'Three-dimensional computer analysis of white shark jaw mechanics: how hard can a great white bite?', Journal of Zoology
- Worm et al. 2013, 'Global catches, exploitation rates, and rebuilding options for sharks', Marine Policy

What scares you more, the shark or the number? Tell us in the comments.
